Leads, not publications: the routine decides what is a commercial real estate dispute between businesses or governments.

2026 IL App (1st) 251339
 No. 1-25-1339
 First Division
 October 13, 2026

 NOTICE: This order was filed under Supreme Court Rule 23 and is not precedent except in the
 limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1).
 ____________________________________________________________________________

 IN THE
 APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS
 FIRST DISTRICT
 ____________________________________________________________________________

 ) Appeal from the
 QUINCY SMITH, ) Circuit Court of
 ) Cook County.
 Plaintiff-Appellee, )
 )
 v. ) No. 23 M1 717869
 )
 QUINN SMITH, )
 ) Honorable
 Defendant-Appellant. ) Gerardo Tristan, Jr.,
 ) Judge, presiding.
 ____________________________________________________________________________

 JUSTICE COBBS delivered the judgment of the court.
 Presiding Justice Ellis and Justice Fitzgerald Smith concurred in the judgment.

 ORDER

¶1 Held: We affirm the circuit court’s eviction order where defendant presented no defenses
 germane to the proceeding and the judgment was not against the manifest weight
 of the evidence.

¶2 Defendant-appellant Quinn Smith appeals from an order of eviction entered against her in

the circuit court of Cook County on June 6, 2025. For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 BACKGROUND
 No. 1-25-1339

¶3 On November 16, 2023, plaintiff-appellee Quincy Smith, defendant’s twin brother, filed a

complaint for eviction against defendant, seeking possession only, of property located at 4940 S.

East End Avenue, #20, Chicago, Illinois. Attached as an exhibit to the complaint was a copy of

the 120-day notice of intent to evict, dated June 11, 2023, indicating that the tenancy would expire

on October 31, 2023. Additionally attached was plaintiff’s affidavit, wherein he averred that there

was “no current lease between the parties with respect to the premises.”

¶4 Notice to defendant of plaintiff’s complaint for eviction was ultimately achieved by posting

on January 29, 2024. Defendant entered her appearance on February 28, 2024. In what would be

defendant’s third motion to dismiss, filed March 28, 2024, she argued that she did not live at the

East End property and attached, as an exhibit, a property tax bill addressed to her for a Colfax

Avenue address in Chicago.

¶5 In his May 29, 2024, response to the motion to dismiss, plaintiff attached as an exhibit a

complaint for discrimination filed by defendant in the United States District Court for the Northern

District of Illinois, captioned “Quinn Smith v. Barclay Condominium Home Owners’

Association.” Relevant here, the federal court complaint alleged that plaintiff, Quinn Smith

(defendant here), is the owner of “a condominium unit at 4940 East End, Unit 20B in Chicago,

Illinois 60615.” The federal court complaint additionally alleged that “on or about 2023,” plaintiff

Quinn and her mother, Odessa Smith, moved into the condominium located on East End Avenue.

On July 2, 2024, the circuit court in this case denied defendant’s motion to dismiss.

¶6 On July 23, 2024, defendant filed her answer, affirmative defenses, and counterclaims

against plaintiff. Among the affirmative defenses, defendant asserted that plaintiff had “unclean

hands," she was not a “bona fide tenant,” and she was a co-owner of the East End property. On

July 31, 2024, plaintiff filed a motion to strike and dismiss defendant’s affirmative defenses and

 -2-
 No. 1-25-1339

counterclaims. Attached as an exhibit to plaintiff’s motion was a copy of a quitclaim deed,

recorded on February 6, 2018, and that identified plaintiff as the sole owner of the East End

property. On September 9, 2024, the circuit court granted plaintiff’s motion to strike and dismiss

defendant’s affirmative defenses and counterclaim.

¶7 On September 20, 2024, plaintiff filed an amended complaint in which he added as a

defendant “Odessa Smith, aka Odessa Norals.” We note, however, that Odessa Smith, who is

plaintiff’s and defendant’s mother, is not a party to this appeal. Defendant filed an answer,

affirmative defenses, asserting improper service, and counterclaims, alleging, inter alia, breach of

warranty of habitability and breach of contract regarding an alleged loan to plaintiff from Odessa

Smith and seeking a declaration on non-tenancy. Added as alternatives were claims for retaliatory

eviction, unjust enrichment, and violations of Chicago’s Residential Landlord and Tenant

Ordinance (“RLTO”). On May 5, 2025, with the exception of defendant’s claim for violation of

the RLTO, the trial court granted plaintiff’s motion to strike and deny defendant’s affirmative

defenses and counterclaims.

¶8 Following the close of discovery, the case proceeded to a bench trial that commenced on

May 29, 2025, and, by court order, continued on June 6, 2025. At the close of evidence, the trial

court entered an order for eviction. Although there is no transcript of the trial proceedings, included

in the record is a certified bystander’s report, dated December 5, 2025, and signed by the presiding

trial judge. See Ill. S. Ct. R. 323 (c) (eff. July 1, 2017).

¶9 Briefly, according to the bystander’s report, on May 29, 2025, immediately after the court

called the case, counsel for defendant stated that his client never lived at the subject property and

asserted to the court that it could grant plaintiff an eviction against the condo unit for all known or

 -3-
 No. 1-25-1339

unknown tenants. However, plaintiff objected. The court then permitted the parties an opportunity

to discuss settlement. No settlement agreement having been reached, the parties proceeded to trial.

¶ 10 Plaintiff first called as a witness Christopher Moore, a process server employed by “It’s

Your Serve.” After being sworn in by the trial judge, Moore testified that he served defendant a

120-day notice. He explained that he knocked on the door of the subject property, defendant

answered the door, and he handed her the 120-day notice. Moore identified defendant in court as

the person he had served. On cross-examination, Moore testified that when defendant answered

the door, he asked who she was, she identified herself, and he then handed her the notice.

¶ 11 Next up to testify was defendant. She stated that she lived at a property on Colfax Avenue

in Chicago that she owns with her mother. She never lived at the East End property, and she never

signed a lease agreement with plaintiff. Upon being shown a lease agreement (Exhibit A), she

stated that it was “a fraudulent lease,” on “metadata” and that the signature that appeared on the

document was not hers. Further, defendant stated that she never applied to the Illinois Rental

Assistance program and that she had never seen the application (Exhibit B). When shown a

cashier’s check for $2,400 made payable “to Quincy Smith for 2 payments of 1200” (Exhibit C),

she acknowledged that the memo on the check stated “Rent,” and that she had written the check

from her business account in order to receive a “write-off on [her] taxes.”

¶ 12 Plaintiff’s testimony essentially contradicted defendant’s testimony regarding the lease

agreement, the cashier’s check, and the rental assistance application. On cross-examination, he

testified that he and defendant applied for rental assistance because defendant wanted to pay him

back some rent payments. He additionally testified that defendant, to whom he had given his proxy

with the condominium homeowner’s association (“HOA”) and management company, was

 -4-
 No. 1-25-1339

“fraudulently telling the HOA and Management that she was the owner of the [ ] unit and causing

all kinds of problems with the building staff, management and HOA.”

¶ 13 Following plaintiff’s testimony, trial was recessed until June 6, 2025. Once trial resumed,

defendant was again called to testify. Her testimony was essentially the same as that given at the

May 29th proceeding.

¶ 14 At the close of the evidence, the trial court recalled the exhibits presented and then

recounted the testimony. The court stated that in light of defendant’s testimony that she “lied to

her bookkeeper to commit fraud on her tax returns,” it was hard to believe her testimony. The court

stated that all of the evidence indicated that defendant had a tenancy at the property and that the

lease had turned into a month-to-month tenancy. The trial judge additionally noted that defendant

admitted that she has “a key and fob and access to the subject property” which confirms that she

is in possession of the property. The court then granted the eviction.

¶ 15 On June 27, 2025, defendant filed a motion to vacate the court’s judgment for possession

to which she attached affidavits from herself and from her mother, Odessa Smith. Both affidavits

averred that defendant did not live at the East End property. On July 1, 2025, defendant filed a

motion to stay enforcement of the eviction order. On July 3, 2025, the court denied defendant’s

motion for stay, and on July 16, 2025, the court denied the motion to vacate the order of eviction.

¶ 16 Included in the record is a stipulation, signed by the parties and filed in the circuit court on

January 16, 2026, which states that the following trial exhibits, inter alia, “were approved in the

certified bystander’s report and were admitted during the proceedings:” “Exhibit A – Lease

Agreement between Quinn and Quincy,” “Exhibit B – Rental Assistance Program Application,”

“Exhibit C - $2400 rent Cashier’s Check,” and “Exhibit D – Text messages Quinn to Quincy.”

 -5-
 No. 1-25-1339

¶ 17 Defendant filed her notice of appeal on July 17, 2025. We have taken the appeal on

defendant’s opening brief and the record only. See First Capitol Mortgage Corp. v. Talandis

Construction Corp., 63 Ill. 2d 128, 133 (1976) (the reviewing court may take a case on appellant’s

brief only). For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 ANALYSIS

¶ 18 Here on appeal, defendant essentially contends that there was no trial as there was no

competent evidence presented to support the court’s judgments. In that regard she argues that no

witnesses were sworn in prior to offering testimony, the lease was not admitted into evidence, and

plaintiff failed to mark or offer any exhibits into evidence. Next, and seemingly her strongest

contention, defendant argues that plaintiff failed to prove the “essential elements necessary to

obtain an order of possession.”

¶ 19 We begin our analysis with a review of defendant’s challenges to procedural errors alleged

to have occurred during the “trial.” With respect to defendant’s argument that no witnesses were

sworn in, we note that the bystander’s report indicates that Moore was sworn in by the court. The

report does not indicate, however, whether the other witnesses, that included plaintiff and

defendant, were also sworn.

¶ 20 It is conceivable to us that the bystander’s report, unlike a transcript of proceedings, does

not reflect verbatim all that was said or done during the proceeding. That said, we also note that

the report does not indicate that any objection was made regarding the court’s alleged failure to

administer oaths to each witness. Thus, we deem any irregularity regarding the administering of

oaths to have been forfeited. Calabrese v. Benitez, 2015 IL App (3d) 130827, ¶ 17 (failure to voice

an objection and to raise the issue in a post-trial motion forfeits the issue on appeal); see 81 Am.

Jur. 2d Witnesses § 633 (August 2026 Update) (“any irregularity in failing to swear a witness is

 -6-
 No. 1-25-1339

waived where the witness is permitted to testify without an objection being interposed”); id. § 634

(although the administration of the oath to a witness is fundamental, absent a timely objection,

unsworn testimony is not a nullity).

¶ 21 Although some authorities state that the failure to swear a witness cannot be dismissed as

a mere irregularity (id. § 633 (August 2026 Update)), our research has found no Illinois case that

so prov

leads.text:
Wilmington Trust, N.A. v Stradtman Park, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05883 
 October 9, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 WILMINGTON TRUST, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION, AS TRUSTEE FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE REGISTERED HOLDERS OF JPMBB COMMERCIAL MORTGAGE SECURITIES TRUST 2014-C24, COMMERCIAL MORTGAGE PASS-THROUGH CERTIFICATES, SERIES 2014-C24, BY AND THROUGH ITS SPECIAL SERVICER, LNR PARTNERS, LLC, PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT, 
 v 
 STRADTMAN PARK, LLC, DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT, ET AL., DEFENDANTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 9, 2026 
 643 CA 25-01133 
 Present: Lindley, J.P., Curran, Ogden, Delconte, And Hannah, JJ. 

 MCCARTER & ENGLISH, LLP, NEW YORK CITY (GREGORY J. MASCITTI OF COUNSEL), FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT. 
 THE SAGE LAW FIRM GROUP PLLC, BUFFALO (KATHRYN FRIEDMAN OF COUNSEL), FOR DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT. 

 Appeal from an amended order and judgment of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Emilio Colaiacovo, J.), entered May 21, 2025, in a mortgage foreclosure action. The amended order and judgment, inter alia, granted plaintiff money damages. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the amended order and judgment so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs. 
 Memorandum: In July 2014, defendant Stradtman Park, LLC (defendant) executed a loan agreement, promissory note, and mortgage and various other documents (loan documents) with nonparty KeyBank National Association (KeyBank) pursuant to which defendant obtained a $3.6 million loan on a commercial property valued at approximately $7 million. The loan documents permitted KeyBank to reassign the loan and to permit securitization through a commercial mortgage-backed security (CMBS) and required defendant to make certain modifications to the loan as required to facilitate the securitization. 
 In October 2014, KeyBank assigned the loan to plaintiff, Wilmington Trust, National Association, as Trustee for the benefit of the registered holders of JPMBB Commercial Mortgage Securities Trust 2014-C24, Commercial Mortgage Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2014-C24 (plaintiff), which placed the loan into a CMBS pursuant to a pooling and servicing agreement (PSA). It is undisputed that defendant was not a signatory to the PSA, and defendant asserts that it was not provided a copy of that document until after this litigation commenced. Pursuant to the PSA, LNR Partners, LLC (LNR) was to act as the special servicer of the loan in the event that defendant's loan became distressed or in default. 
 From 2014 through early 2020, defendant paid all amounts required by the loan documents. Specifically, defendant was required to pay principal and interest in the amount of $18,779.30 per month and reserve account payments, which were funds for taxes, insurance, maintenance, repairs, etc., in the amount of $20,300.39 per month, for a monthly total payment of $39,079.69. 
 At some point in 2019, defendant requested approval for lease renewals, expansions, contractor repair payments, and other relief required to be paid from the reserve accounts [*2] pursuant to the loan documents. Although the loan was neither distressed nor in default, LNR became the contact entity for such requests. According to defendant, LNR was dilatory and obstructionist with all of defendant's legitimate requests and, as a result, defendant was forced to pay certain amounts itself, despite having ample reserve funds to make those payments. 
 Defendant began paying only the principal and interest on the loan in May 2020 and withheld the reserve amounts, directing that its monthly payments of $18,779.30 be applied toward principal and interest only. Plaintiff or LNR, however, spread those payments over principal, interest, and reserve payments, resulting in defendant's default. In November 2020, defendant stopped remitting the rental payment proceeds required by the loan documents to plaintiff, which later commenced this action seeking, inter alia, to foreclose on the mortgage. 
 Supreme Court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment with respect to the first and third causes of action, i.e., mortgage foreclosure and entitlement to rents. That order is not challenged on appeal. Questioning many of the fees sought to be recovered by plaintiff, the court directed a hearing on damages. Plaintiff appeals from the subsequent amended order and judgment, contending that the court erred in its determinations with respect to certain damages and fees. We now affirm. 
 At hearings or inquests regarding damages, "the plaintiff bears the burden of setting forth a prima facie case as to damages" ( Bobbo Prop. Mgt. , Inc. v Faulkner , 235 AD3d 615 , 615 [2d Dept 2025]; see Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy. , FSB v Moriarty-Gentile , 242 AD3d 1150 , 1152 [2d Dept 2025]), and, on an appeal from a nonjury hearing or trial, "this Court 'has authority . . . as broad as that of the trial court . . . and . . . may render the judgment it finds warranted by the facts' . . . 'Nonetheless, the decision of the fact-finding court should not be disturbed upon appeal unless it is obvious that the court's conclusions could not be reached under any fair interpretation of the evidence' " ( DiMarco Constructors , LLC v Top Capital of N.Y. Brockport , LLC , 236 AD3d 1342 , 1343 [4th Dept 2025]; see Estate of Sonnelitter v Estate of White [appeal No. 2], 115 AD3d 1160, 1162 [4th Dept 2014]). 
 Although there is a " 'sound rule in the construction of contracts, that where the language is clear, unequivocal and unambiguous, the contract is to be interpreted by its own language' " ( R/S Assoc. v New York Job Dev. Auth ., 98 NY2d 29, 32 [2002], quoting Springsteen v Samson , 32 NY 703 , 706 [1865]), we note that " '[a] foreclosure action is equitable in nature and triggers the equitable powers of the court' . . . '[O]nce equity is invoked, the court's power is as broad as equity and justice require' " ( Meadowlands Portfolio , LLC v Manton , 118 AD3d 1439, 1440 [4th Dept 2014]; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Losner , 145 AD3d 935, 938 [2d Dept 2016]). 
 Here, plaintiff contends that the court erred in denying it recovery of note rate interest in the amount of $120,882.59, in addition to the default rate interest of $583,938.25 awarded by the court. Contrary to plaintiff's contention, it was not entitled to both note rate interest and default rate interest inasmuch as the default rate was set at five percent above the note rate and the court awarded plaintiff the exact amount of default rate interest it requested. Because plaintiff did not establish with documentary evidence how the default rate interest it requested was calculated, we conclude that the court's determination that it would be duplicative to award both default rate interest and note rate interest is supported by a fair interpretation of the evidence. 
 We reject plaintiff's further contention that the court abused its discretion in determining the amount of the attorneys' fees awarded. Defendant did not dispute that plaintiff and LNR were entitled to attorneys' fees, but it contested the reasonableness of the requested fees, relying on expert testimony regarding reasonable fees for commercial mortgage foreclosure actions in Western New York. Defendant's expert opined that a "customary, reasonable" fee for an experienced attorney in commercial foreclosure proceedings in Western New York would range from $350 to $450 an hour. Plaintiff's sole witness testified that LNR was paying between $650-800 an hour for the services of law firm partners and between $350-575 an hour for associates. None of the attorney invoices submitted by plaintiff delineated the rate for each charge. Plaintiff requested approximately $588,000 in attorneys' fees, but the court awarded only $250,000, finding that the rates requested by plaintiff were unreasonable and that numerous charges were "duplicative and exaggerated." Indeed, the court noted that plaintiff had come "perilously close" to having the entire judgment vacated due to its exorbitant request for attorneys' fees. 
 An award of attorneys' fees, even if permitted by contract, " 'may only be enforced to the extent that the amount is reasonable and warranted for the services actually rendered' " ( SO/Bluestar , LLC v Canarsie Hotel Corp ., 33 AD3d 986, 987 [2d Dept 2006]). Such a determination involves a review of the number of hours spent on the case, the hourly rate that was being charged, and the customary fees charged for services by lawyers in the community with like experience and reputation ( see Matakov v Kel-Tech Constr. Inc ., 84 AD3d 677, 678 [1st Dept 2011]; Wells v Crosson , 210 AD2d 932, 932 [4th Dept 1994]; Getty Petroleum Corp. v G.M. Triple S. Corp ., 187 AD2d 483, 483-484 [2d Dept 1992]). We conclude that the court's determination to award $250,000 was not an abuse of discretion and should not be disturbed. 
 We have reviewed plaintiff's remaining challenges to the court's determinations with respect to the awards of damages and fees and conclude that all the challenged determinations are based on a fair interpretation of the evidence and that none of those challenges warrants modification or reversal of the amended order and judgment. 
 Entered: October 9, 2026 
 Ann Dillon Flynn 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.text:
RECOMMENDED FOR PUBLICATION
 Pursuant to Sixth Circuit I.O.P. 32.1(b)
 File Name: 26a0281p.06

 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
 FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT

 ┐
 LEXON INSURANCE COMPANY,
 │
 Plaintiff-Appellee, │
 > No. 25-6096
 │
 v. │
 │
 JAMES C. JUSTICE, II, │
 Defendant-Appellant. │
 ┘

 Appeal from the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee at Nashville.
 No. 3:23-cv-00772—Waverly D. Crenshaw, Jr., District Judge.

 Argued: July 30, 2026

 Decided and Filed: October 9, 2026

 Before: STRANCH, BUSH, and MURPHY, Circuit Judges.
 _________________

 COUNSEL

ARGUED: David R. Pogue, CAREY DOUGLAS KESSLER & RUBY, PLLC, Charleston,
West Virginia, for Appellant. Jason M. Halper, VINSON & ELKINS LLP, New York, New
York, for Appellee. ON BRIEF: David R. Pogue, Steven R. Ruby, CAREY DOUGLAS
KESSLER & RUBY, PLLC, Charleston, West Virginia, Peter C. Robison, LEWIS
THOMASON P.C., Nashville, Tennessee, for Appellant. Jason M. Halper, Sara E. Brauerman,
Timbre L. Shriver, VINSON & ELKINS LLP, New York, New York, W. Brantley Phillips, Jr.,
Garrah Carter-Mason, BASS, BERRY & SIMS PLC, Nashville, Tennessee, for Appellee.
 _________________

 OPINION
 _________________

 MURPHY, Circuit Judge. Senator James C. Justice II and his family own and operate
several coal companies. These companies obtained bonds from Lexon Insurance Company.
  No. 25-6096 Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice Page 2

After the companies fell behind on their premium payments for the bonds, they signed a contract
with Lexon agreeing to get up to speed. Senator Justice personally guaranteed these payments as
well. But the companies still did not pay the agreed-upon amounts. Lexon thus sued Justice
under his personal guaranty. The district court held him liable for about $25 million. Justice
now raises arguments about the meaning of the contract and the guaranty to challenge a portion
of this award. Yet we agree with the district court’s readings of these documents. We thus
affirm.

 I

 States typically prohibit coal companies from mining coal without a permit. To obtain a
permit, a company often must secure a surety bond. “A surety bond is a tripartite contract.” Tr.,
R.119, PageID 1956. The insured (typically, a coal company) owes duties of performance to an
“obligee” (typically, a state agency). Id., PageID 1956–57. When applying for a permit, for
example, coal companies often promise to restore the mined land “to its preexisting condition”
after they complete their operations. Id., PageID 1957. And the surety (typically, an insurer)
will “guarantee the faithful performance” of the insured’s duties, including this reclamation duty.
Id. Unlike a typical insurer, a surety cannot “cancel[]” a bond on its own if a company fails to
pay the premiums. Id., PageID 1959–60. So the bond “remains in full force” until the obligee
releases it or the company meets its obligations. Id., PageID 1959–60, 1963. Also unlike a
typical insurer, the surety may seek reimbursement from companies if they fail “to honor their
obligations” and thereby require the surety to cover them. Id., PageID 1959.

 This case involves two of the three parties to the surety-bond relationship. “Lexon is a
surety bond provider.” Id., PageID 1953. When Lexon issues a surety bond to a coal company,
it assumes the risk that the company might breach its reclamation duties at the end of the mining.
This bond thus exposes Lexon to potentially massive liability. Lexon takes two steps to mitigate
its financial exposure. It requires coal companies seeking a bond to agree to pay annual
premiums. And Lexon requires these companies to post adequate collateral that it may use for
reimbursement if the companies require it to pay for any of their obligations.
  No. 25-6096 Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice Page 3

 Several coal companies and affiliates owned by Senator Justice and his family (along
with one other affiliate) sit on the insured side of the surety relationship. We will call all these
entities “the Companies.” The Companies began to obtain surety bonds from Lexon in 2010.
The bonds exposed Lexon to the Companies’ obligations to regulators, which have consistently
exceeded $100 million in risk. When creating each bond, Lexon and the Companies entered into
general indemnity agreements. These agreements required the Companies to pay annual
premiums.

 The Companies’ financial condition has deteriorated during their relationship with
Lexon. They paid their premiums on time for years. Over the past decade, however, the coal
industry has faced a “difficult” environment and “depressed” coal market. Tr., R.120, PageID
2213–14. As a result, the Companies started to miss premium payments around 2016. Lexon
responded by requiring them to set aside collateral. This collateral eventually reached almost
$20 million. By early 2018, the collateral had declined to about $5 million. And although the
Companies still had not made all their required premium payments, they sought to reduce the
collateral even more.

 In March 2018, therefore, Lexon and the Companies signed an agreement designed to
release the Companies’ collateral and help them catch up on past-due premiums. Lexon agreed
to release $5 million of collateral so that the Companies could pay down certain debts (including
reclamation expenses that would reduce various Lexon-backed obligations). In exchange, the
Companies agreed to post $5 million in new collateral within six months and to pay the $3
million they owed in past-due premiums within two months. As a condition to this agreement,
Lexon required Senator Justice to personally guarantee the Companies’ duties to provide the
collateral and pay the premiums.

 By early 2019, though, the Companies still had not met their obligations under this
agreement. They had failed to post any of the $5 million in collateral. And they still owed
$1.025 million in past-due premiums.

 Lexon and the Companies thus entered what we will call the “Amended Agreement”—
the one that matters for this appeal—in February 2019. This agreement modified both the
  No. 25-6096 Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice Page 4

Companies’ collateral obligations and their premium obligations. As for the collateral
obligations, the Amended Agreement required the Companies to post $20 million in new
collateral by April 1, 2021. They agreed to fund this collateral in the allotted time by paying
monthly installments of $250,000, selling some equipment, and making larger periodic payments
on certain dates.

 As for the premium obligations, the Amended Agreement first identified the amounts that
the Companies owed. It calculated the “Remaining Indebtedness” (the amount that the
Companies owed under the prior agreement) as $1,025,000. Joint App’x (J.A.) 151. In the
meantime, though, the Companies had continued to miss premium payments. The Amended
Agreement thus made clear that “additional premium of $2,513,400.75 [was then] due and owing
(the ‘New Indebtedness’).” Id. The Amended Agreement also contemplated that “additional
amounts for premium may become due during the term of this Agreement,” so this New
Indebtedness would increase if the Companies missed current premium payments by 60 days.
Id. at 152–53. The Amended Agreement added: “The Remaining Indebtedness together with the
New Indebtedness is equal to $3,538,400.75 (the ‘Total Indebtedness’).” Id. at 151. The
Companies agreed to pay $200,000 a month toward this “Total Indebtedness” until it was “paid
in full[.]” Id.

 Before entering into this agreement with the Companies, Lexon required Senator Justice
to give another personal guaranty. If the Companies breached the Amended Agreement, Justice
promised to repay the amounts of unpaid collateral and premiums due “within three (3) business
days” of receiving Lexon’s written demand. J.A. 139. But the guaranty capped Justice’s
payment obligations. As relevant here, it “limited” his liability “to a total sum equal to (i) twenty
million U.S. dollars ($20,000,000.00) plus (ii) the amount of the Total Indebtedness specified in
the” Amended Agreement. J.A. 141–42.

 Unfortunately, the Companies’ conditions did not improve after the Amended
Agreement. When they continued to struggle to make timely payments, they asked Lexon for an
amended payment schedule. Lexon consented twice. In two side letter agreements from January
and March 2020, it adjusted the Companies’ payment obligations. Lexon suspended the
obligation to make the monthly $250,000 collateral payment for six months, pushing back the
  No. 25-6096 Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice Page 5

requirement to pay the full $20 million to October 1, 2021. But Lexon asked the Companies to
temporarily increase their premium payments. The $200,000 monthly amount was not “closing
the gap” on the total past-due premiums because the Companies were failing to pay all their
current premiums (which became past due after 60 days). J.A. 298. The January 2020 side
agreement thus required the Companies to make six monthly premium payments of $250,000
(not $200,000).

 Even after entering into these additional letter agreements, the Companies still could not
meet their collateral and premium obligations. Ultimately, the Companies paid only $5.75
million of the $20 million they owed in collateral and made no collateral payments after
December 2019. Similarly, the Companies paid $4.21 million in premiums starting in February
2019, but they stopped making any premium payments in March 2021. Lexon thus sent the
Companies default letters that demanded payment on the outstanding collateral and premiums.
Yet the Companies never paid the entire amounts owed.

 When the Companies did not pay, Lexon turned to Senator Justice. In July 2023, Lexon
sent him a letter demanding payment of the outstanding collateral and premium obligations plus
interest. Under the guaranty, Justice had three days to satisfy these amounts. But he declined as
well.

 Lexon thus sued Justice to enforce the guaranty. At the summary-judgment stage, the
district court largely ruled for Lexon. See Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice, 2024 WL 4960006, at *21
(M.D. Tenn. Dec. 3, 2024). It held that Justice breached the guaranty as a matter of law when he
failed to pay upon Lexon’s written demand. See id. at *5–7. But it also held that a genuine issue
of material fact existed on Lexon’s damages. See id. at *8. The guaranty limited Justice’s
liability to a combination of $20,000,000.00 for the collateral plus the amount of the Total
Indebtedness on the past-due premiums. See id. The court concluded as a matter of law that
Justice owed $14.25 million for the collateral ($20 million minus the $5.75 million that the
Companies already paid). See id. at *11. But it found a dispute of fact over the amount of
“Total Indebtedness” owed to Lexon for past-due premiums. See id.
  No. 25-6096 Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice Page 6

 The court held a two-day bench trial on damages. See Lexon Ins. Co. v. Justice, 808
F. Supp. 3d 841, 845 (M.D. Tenn. 2025). It recognized that the initial “Total Indebtedness” (the
amount of overdue premiums) equaled $3,538,400.75 at the time of the Amended Agreement.
See id. at 851. It also recognized that the Companies had paid $4.21 million in premium
payments—more than the initial amount of Total Indebtedness. See id. at 852. But it interpreted
the phrase “Total Indebtedness” to represent a dynamic figure that would increase every time the
Companies missed a current premium payment by 60 days. See id. at 853–62. It next held that
the Amended Agreement’s “term” extended until the Companies “paid” the collateral and
premium obligations “in full.” Id. at 863–67. These interpretations clarified the amount of Total
Indebtedness owed. Since the Amended Agreement’s start in February 2019, the Companies had
accrued $7,391,308.49 in additional tardy premiums. Id. at 867. The Total Indebtedness thus
equaled $10,929,709.24 (the initial $3,538,400.75 plus $7,391,308.49). See id. (According to
the testimony of a Lexon witness, thi

leads.caseName: Texas Captl Bank v. Govt Natl Mtge
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
leads.text:
Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 1 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 United States Court of Appeals
 for the Fifth Circuit
 United States Court of Appeals
 Fifth Circuit

 ____________ FILED
 October 9, 2026
 No. 25-10624 Thomas B. Plunkett, III
 ____________ Clerk

Texas Capital Bank,

 Plaintiff—Appellant,

 versus

Government National Mortgage Association; United
States Department of Housing and Urban Development,

 Defendants—Appellees.
 ______________________________

 Appeal from the United States District Court
 for the Northern District of Texas
 USDC No. 2:23-cv-156
 ______________________________

Before Elrod, Chief Judge, Willett and Wilson, Circuit Judges.
Cory T. Wilson, Circuit Judge:
 Under Ginnie Mae’s Home Equity Conversion Mortgage-Backed
Securities (HMBS) program, mortgage issuers securitize federally insured
reverse mortgages while retaining certain interests in the underlying loans,
including an interest in subsequent borrower advances known in the industry
as “tails.” This case concerns what happens to a third-party lender’s
security interest in mortgage tails when, by operation of contract and federal
 Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 2 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

law, Ginnie Mae assumes a bankrupt issuer’s interests in its underlying
securitized mortgages.
 Reverse Mortgage Funding, LLC (RMF) participated in the HMBS
program. When RMF entered bankruptcy, Texas Capital Bank provided
debtor-in-possession financing to RMF, secured by RMF’s interests in
certain collateral, including its Home Equity Conversion Mortgage
(HECM) tails. After RMF defaulted on the guaranty agreement between
them, Ginnie Mae, exercising its statutory and contractual authority,
eventually extinguished RMF’s interests in the underlying mortgages and
assumed ownership of the loans.
 The parties hotly dispute whether Ginnie Mae’s extinguishment of
RMF’s mortgage interests properly encompassed Texas Capital’s lien on
RMF’s mortgage tails. Ginnie Mae says it did. Texas Capital counters with
claims that Ginnie Mae’s position violates the Administrative Procedure Act
(APA) and Texas tort law. The district court dismissed Texas Capital’s
promissory estoppel claim, declined to consider its arbitrary and capricious
theory, and later dismissed its statutory authority and tortious interference
claims via summary judgment. We affirm.
 I.
 A.
 This case involves the interaction of two federal housing programs:
the HECM program, administered by the Department of Housing and
Urban Development (HUD), see 12 U.S.C. § 1715z-20(a)(1), and the

 2
  Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

HMBS program, administered by the Government National Mortgage
Association (Ginnie Mae),1 see 12 U.S.C. § 1716.
 The HECM program is a federally insured reverse mortgage program
designed to allow elderly homeowners to convert home equity into cash while
continuing to live in their homes. Under the program, a lender provides a
loan secured by the borrower’s home equity, and the Federal Housing
Authority (FHA) insures those loans. Under the HMBS program, FHA-
approved HECM lenders (or issuers) are then able to pool and securitize
their loans via government-backed securities.
 A single HECM loan can generate several distinct financial interests
over time. When an issuer securitizes a HECM loan, it typically pools part
of the loan’s principal balance into a HMBS pool, which Ginnie Mae
guarantees. The pooled amounts are known as “participations.”
 HECM loans often accrue additional balances after securitization.
Reverse mortgages allow borrowers to draw additional funds against home
equity over time, so new advances, interest accruals, insurance premiums,
and other charges may increase the mortgage balance after the initial
securitization date. These additional amounts are referred to as “tails,” and
they are unsecuritized. No tail can exist unless an underlying securitized
HECM loan precedes it.

 _____________________
 1
 Ginnie Mae is a government-owned association within HUD. Ginnie Mae
guarantees securities backed by federally insured or guaranteed mortgages, with the goal of
expanding affordable housing. 12 U.S.C. § 1717(b)(1).

 3
 Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 4 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

 To participate in the HMBS program, issuers execute a guaranty
agreement with Ginnie Mae. See 12 U.S.C. § 1721(g)(1). The agreement
governs the relationship between Ginnie Mae and the issuer, and it defines
the parties’ respective rights in the underlying mortgage loans.
 B.
 RMF participated in the HMBS program. RMF originated HECM
loans and issued securities backed by pools of its loans. Under its guaranty
agreement with Ginnie Mae, executed in July 2021, RMF conveyed all title
and interest in securitized HECM loans to Ginnie Mae. Ginnie Mae then
assigned specific rights and interests back to RMF to allow RMF to service
the mortgages. Section 10.04 of the guaranty agreement expressly provides
that upon RMF’s default, Ginnie Mae could, by letter, “automatically effect
and complete the extinguishment of any redemption, equitable, legal, or
other right, title, or interest of the Issuer in the Mortgages, the related Ginnie
Participations and any Other Interests.”
 In late 2022, RMF experienced a severe liquidity crisis and filed for
Chapter 11 bankruptcy. RMF’s bankruptcy constituted an “immediate
default” under its guaranty agreement with Ginnie Mae. Despite RMF’s
default, Ginnie Mae did not immediately extinguish RMF’s interests.
Instead, Ginnie Mae sought to negotiate a resolution that would allow
RMF’s mortgage-servicing platform and loan portfolio to be transferred to
another market participant.
 To continue operations during the bankruptcy proceedings, RMF
sought debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing from a third-party lender.
Texas Capital ultimately agreed to provide RMF with over $28 million in
secured DIP financing. Texas Capital’s loan was secured not by the pooled
mortgage participations themselves, but by the incremental balances
accruing after securitization (i.e., the tails), per the Fifth Amended and

 4
  Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 5 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

Restated Loan and Security Agreement (the Tail Agreement) between RMF
and Texas Capital.2 The bankruptcy court approved this arrangement,
granting Texas Capital “first priority valid, perfected, enforceable and
unavoidable liens on, and security interest in, the existing collateral secured
under the [Tail Agreement].”
 According to Texas Capital, Ginnie Mae originally made verbal
assurances that Texas Capital would retain its interest in the DIP collateral
(i.e., the tails), even if Ginnie Mae extinguished RMF’s interests. Ginnie
Mae disputes that it provided such assurances and instead asserts that, in
both emails and formal correspondence, it warned Texas Capital that making
such a promise would be outside the scope of Ginnie Mae’s authority.
 Negotiations among RMF, Ginnie Mae, and other stakeholders
ultimately failed to yield a feasible transferee for RMF’s HECM portfolio.
Faced with RMF’s continuing default, Ginnie Mae terminated RMF from
the HMBS program and extinguished RMF’s rights and interests in the
mortgages, citing the guaranty agreement. In doing so, Ginnie Mae
purported also to extinguish Texas Capital’s separate lien interest in the loan
tails. This in turn gave rise to the central dispute in this case: whether Ginnie
Mae’s authority to extinguish RMF’s interests in the HECM mortgages
also permitted it to eliminate Texas Capital’s lien interest in the pledged DIP
financing collateral, i.e., the HECM tails.

 _____________________
 2
 The Tail Agreement defined a tail as “the aggregate of any additional amounts,
including but not limited to amounts created by additional draws by the Obligor, interest
accruals, mortgage insurance premiums, fees, or charges, which accrue, are disbursed, or
are added to the balance of a previously-securitized HECM Loan after the closing date of
any prior securitization of the HECM Loan or any prior HECM Tail related thereto.”

 5
  Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 6 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

 C.
 Texas Capital sued Ginnie Mae and HUD (collectively hereafter,
Ginnie Mae) in the Northern District of Texas in October 2023. Texas
Capital alleged three claims: violation of the APA, promissory estoppel
under Texas law, and tortious interference with property under Texas law.
Ginnie Mae responded with a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 12(b)(6), arguing that Texas Capital’s APA claim failed because
Ginnie Mae acted within its statutory authority in extinguishing Texas
Capital’s lien and that sovereign immunity barred Texas Capital’s state law
claims. Ginnie Mae also asserted that Texas Capital’s tortious interference
claim failed on the merits because Ginnie Mae had the legal right to take the
challenged actions. Opposing the motion, Texas Capital asserted, inter alia,
that its APA claim encompassed two distinct theories, namely that Ginnie
Mae exceeded its statutory authority, and acted arbitrarily and capriciously.
 The district court granted Ginnie Mae’s motion in part and denied it
in part. The court concluded that Texas Capital plausibly alleged that Ginnie
Mae lacked statutory authority to extinguish Texas Capital’s interest in
RMF’s loans and likewise determined that the tortious interference claim
could proceed. The court declined to construe Texas Capital’s complaint as
asserting a separate arbitrary-and-capricious APA claim and thus refused to
consider that theory.3 The court also dismissed Texas Capital’s promissory
estoppel claim as barred by sovereign immunity and improperly pled.
 After Ginnie Mae produced its administrative record, Texas Capital
moved for summary judgment as to the APA statutory authority claim. The

 _____________________
 3
 Texas Capital never attempted to amend its complaint in the district court to
allege an express arbitrary-and-capricious claim. Nor has Texas Capital attempted to
amend its complaint on appeal.

 6
  Case: 25-10624 Document: 83-1 Page: 7 Date Filed: 10/09/2026

 No. 25-10624

district court denied the motion, instead concluding that Ginnie Mae acted
within its statutory authority and that Ginnie Mae’s extinguishment of
RMF’s interests necessarily extinguished any remaining derivative interest
that Texas Capital had in the underlying mortgages.
 Ginnie Mae then moved for summary judgment “on all remaining
claims.” The district court obliged, holding that Ginnie Mae acted within its
statutory authority and that, as a result, the tortious interference claim failed
too.
 Texas Capital appealed.
 II.
 In this court, Texas Capital renews its contentions that Ginnie Mae
(1) exceeded its statutory authority under the APA, (2) tortiously interfered
with Texas Capital’s property under Texas law, and (3) acted arbitrarily and
capriciously under the APA.4 As for the first two claims, this court reviews
de novo “a district court’s grant of summary judgment and questions of
statutory interpretation.” Seago v. O’Malley, 91 F.4th 386, 389 (5th Cir.
2024) (citation omitted). Summary judgment is appropriate when “there is
no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to
judgment as a matter of law.” FED. R. CIV. P. 56(a).
 “‘[A]gency interpretations of statutes’ are reviewed without
deference.” Texas v. EPA, 156 F.4th 523, 536 (5th Cir. 2025) (quoting Loper
Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 392 (2024)). “The interpretation
of an unambiguous contract is a matter of law,” and “a district court may

 _____________________
 4
 Texas Capital’s briefing on appeal does not mention the promissory-estoppel
theory, so it is forfeited. See Banks v. Thaler, 583 F.3d 295, 329 (5th Cir. 2009) (“It is well
established . . . that an appellant abandons all issues not raised and properly presented in its
initial brief on appeal.”).

 7

leads.caseName: Alliance for the Wild Rockies v. United States Forest Service
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
leads.text:
FOR PUBLICATION

 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
 FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT

ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD No. 25-3518
ROCKIES,
 D.C. No.
 2:21-cv-00244-
 Plaintiff - Appellee,
 REP
 v.

UNITED STATES FOREST
SERVICE, an agency of the U.S. OPINION
Department of Agriculture;
TIMOTHY GILLOON, in his official
capacity as Supervisor of the Idaho
Panhandle National Forests,

 Defendants - Appellants.

 Appeal from the United States District Court
 for the District of Idaho
Raymond Edward Patricco, Jr., Magistrate Judge, Presiding

 Argued and Submitted June 3, 2026
 Seattle, Washington

 Filed October 9, 2026

 Before: Ryan D. Nelson, Danielle J. Forrest, and Jennifer
 Sung, Circuit Judges.

 Opinion by Judge R. Nelson
 2 ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS

 SUMMARY *

 National Forest Management Act

 The panel reversed the district court’s summary
judgment in favor of the Alliance for the Wild Rockies in the
Alliance’s action challenging the Hanna Flats Good
Neighbor Authority Project (the Project), which seeks to
manage vegetation and reduce fuels in the Idaho Panhandle
National Forest.
 Under the National Forest Management Act (NFMA),
the United States Forest Service must ensure that its projects
in the Idaho Panhandle National Forest are consistent with a
document called the Access Amendments, which limits the
miles of roads constructed in areas in and around bear
habitat. The Access Amendments regulate four categories
of roads: permanent open roads, temporary open roads,
permanent total roads, and temporary total roads. The
Access Amendments cap road mileage in the Priest Bears
Outside Recovery Zone (BORZ) at a baseline set in
2011. The district court concluded that the Project violated
the Access Amendments, and therefore the NFMA, because
total post-project mileage (338.8 miles) would exceed the
2011 baseline (316.4 miles).
 The panel held that the court’s decision in Alliance for
the Wild Rockies v. Higgins, 183 F.4th 671 (9th Cir. 2026),
did not render the appeal moot.

*
 This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court. It has
been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader.
  ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS 3

 Turning to the merits, the panel first considered whether
the Project was consistent with provisions of the Access
Amendments controlling the construction of permanent
roads. The panel held that the district court erred in
considering only the number of noncompliant miles in the
Priest BORZ without reference to the causal relationship
between those noncompliant miles and the Project. The
Forest Service showed that the entire difference between the
post-project 338.8 miles of total roads and the Access
Amendments’ baseline of 316.4 miles was not caused or
contributed to by the Project. Accordingly, the district court
erred by finding that the Project was inconsistent with the
permanent road requirements in the Access Amendments.
 Second, the panel held that Alliance failed to show that
the Project was inconsistent with the temporary road
provisions of the Access Amendments. Alliance’s argument
that the temporary road provisions obligated the Forest
Service to remediate BORZ-wide background
noncompliance failed because that provision governed only
the temporary roads a project uses. Alliance’s challenges to
the Forest Service’s road-closure practices failed absent any
factual finding to the contrary.
 Accordingly, the panel reversed the district court’s order
and remanded for further proceedings.
 4 ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS

 COUNSEL

Rebecca K. Smith (argued), Public Interest Defense Center
PC, Missoula, Montana, for Plaintiff-Appellee.
Jacob D. Ecker (argued), Thekla Hansen-Young, John P.
Tustin, and Emma L. Hamilton, Attorneys, Environment &
Natural Resources Division; Adam R.F. Gustafson,
Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General; United States
Department of Justice, Washington, D.C.; Nicholas Pino and
Charles Spicknall, Attorneys, United States Department of
Agriculture, Washington, D.C.; Justin D. Whatcott,
Assistant United States Attorney, Office of the United States
Attorney, United States Department of Justice, Boise, Idaho;
for Defendants-Appellants.

 OPINION

R. NELSON, Circuit Judge:

 Under the National Forest Management Act (NFMA),
the Forest Service must ensure that its projects in the Idaho
Panhandle National Forest are consistent with a document
called the Access Amendments, which limits the miles of
roads constructed in areas in and around bear habitat. The
Access Amendments cap road mileage in the Priest Bears
Outside Recovery Zone (BORZ) at a baseline set in 2011.
 Appellee Alliance for the Wild Rockies (Alliance)
challenges the Hanna Flats Good Neighbor Authority
Project (Hanna Flats Project, or the Project), which seeks to
manage vegetation and reduce fuels in the Idaho Panhandle
National Forest. The Project reduces road mileage in the
  ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS 5

BORZ by 1.2 miles. But the Priest BORZ currently contains
another 23.6 miles of road that were discovered after 2011
but before the Project. Alliance asserts that these additional
miles of roads cause the Project to violate NFMA and the
Access Amendments.
 The district court granted summary judgment for
Alliance, concluding that the Project violated the Access
Amendments and therefore NFMA because total post-
project mileage (338.8 miles) would exceed the 2011
baseline (316.4 miles). The Forest Service appeals, arguing
that the district court erred by failing to address whether the
Project caused or worsened any noncompliance with the
2011 baseline.
 We agree with the Forest Service. Under Lands Council
v. Powell, 395 F.3d 1019, 1035–36 (9th Cir. 2005), a project
is consistent with a forest plan when the project does not
cause or contribute to noncompliance; we exclude from
analysis preexisting background noncompliance caused by
other factors. The district court applied a straight before-
and-after comparison and never considered causation. That
was error. The Forest Service has determined that 23.6 miles
of road were on the ground but omitted from the 2011
baseline survey and that the Project reduces the recorded
baseline mileage by 1.2 miles.
 We reverse the district court’s grant of summary
judgment and remand for further proceedings consistent
with this opinion.
 I
 A
 Congress passed the National Forest Management Act
(NFMA) to ensure “a comprehensive assessment of present
 6 ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS

and anticipated uses, demand for, and supply of renewable
resources from the Nation’s public and private forests.” 16
U.S.C. § 1600(3). But few arborists get elected, so Congress
delegated much of the work for managing the Nation’s
forests to the United States Forest Service. “NFMA and its
implementing regulations provide for forest planning and
management by the Forest Service on two levels: (1) forest
level and (2) individual project level.” Native Ecosystems
Council v. Weldon, 697 F.3d 1043, 1056 (9th Cir. 2012).
 NFMA requires the Forest Service to “develop,
maintain, and, as appropriate, revise land and resource
management plans for units of the National Forest System.”
16 U.S.C. § 1604(a). This is the forest level of NFMA. At
this level, the “Forest Service develops a Land and Resource
Management Plan (forest plan), which consists of broad,
long-term plans and objectives for the entire forest.”
Weldon, 697 F.3d at 1056. “After a forest plan is approved,
the Forest Service implements the forest plan when
approving or denying site-specific projects.” Id. When
implementing site-specific projects, “the Forest Service’s
failure to comply with the provisions of a Forest Plan is a
violation of NFMA.” Native Ecosystems Council v. U.S.
Forest Serv., 418 F.3d 953, 961 (9th Cir. 2005); see also 16
U.S.C. § 1604(i).
 Alliance alleges that the Project does not comply with
the Idaho Panhandle National Forest Land and Resource
Management Plan (IPN Forest Plan), which governs projects
within the Idaho Panhandle National Forest (IPN Forest).
The IPN Forest Plan sets several objectives for the IPN
Forest, including habitat conservation for grizzly bears.
Higher densities of motorized roads drive grizzly bears from
their preferred habitat and lead to more bear–human
conflicts.
  ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS 7

 Over twenty years ago, Alliance was concerned that the
IPN Forest Plan did not do enough to prevent these
encounters. So it sued, seeking to reduce the number of
roads in grizzly bear habitats. That lawsuit prompted the
Forest Service to make some changes. In 2011, the Forest
Service amended the IPN Forest Plan to alter the road
density in grizzly bear habitat, through a document referred
to as the Access Amendments. The Access Amendments
established two types of areas in which it would restrict the
total linear miles of motorized roads to protect grizzly bears:
Grizzly Bear Recovery Zones, the primary bear habitat, and
Bears Outside Recovery Zones (BORZ), adjacent areas
where curious bears are known to wander. This case
concerns the BORZ for the region around Priest River.
 As to roads, the Access Amendments require that “there
be no increases in permanent linear miles of open road and
no net permanent increases in linear miles of total roads” in
BORZs. To accomplish this, the Access Amendments
provide that “[l]inear miles of open road in a given area will
not be able to go above the defined baseline conditions
displayed in Table 16 of Appendix B,” which establishes a
baseline of 316.4 Total Linear Miles of Road in the Priest
BORZ and 314.4 Linear Miles of Open Road in the Priest
BORZ. The Access Amendments require the Forest Service
to conduct yearly monitoring and report progress made
toward the goals of the Amendments as well as any changes
in the on-the-ground conditions.
 The Access Amendments regulate four categories of
roads: permanent open roads, temporary open roads,
permanent total roads, and temporary total roads. If the
Forest Service chooses to construct or authorize new miles
of road in a BORZ, the way those roads count against the
 8 ALLIANCE FOR THE WILD ROCKIES V. USFS

Table 16 baselines differs according to the conditions set for
each type of road.
 Permanent Open Roads. These roads are open year-
round and accessible to the public using motorized vehicles.
The Access Amendments provide that the Forest Service
“shall ensure no increases in permanent linear miles of open
road on National Forest System lands in any individual
BORZ, above the baseline conditions” identified in a
baseline set in 2011 and specified in Table 16 of Appendix
B. 1 The Forest Service may build new roads, but
“[p]otential increases in linear miles of open roads must be
compensated for with in-kind reductions in linear miles of
open road concurrently with, or prior to, project
implementation within the same BORZ.”
 Temporary Open Roads. The Forest Service can also
build new open roads if they are temporary. “Temporary
increases in linear miles of open roads are acceptable” in the
BORZ under defined conditions, but only during the bear
summer season (June 16 through August 31) and only when

1
 The relevant provision of the Access Amendments provides that “[t]he
Forest [Service] shall ensure no increases in permanent linear miles of
open road on National Forest System lands in any individual BORZ,
above the baseline conditions identified in Table 4.” But all parallel
provisions of the Access Amendments reference Table 16 of Appendix
B. Table 4 in the Access Amendments does not include baselines for
individual BORZs, but as we explained in Alliance for the Wild Rockies
v. Bradford, 856 F.3d 1238, 1240–42 (9th Cir. 2017), Table 4 of the
Biological Opinion prepared by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
concurrently with the Access Amendments is identical to Table 16 of the
Access Amendments. We thus treat this reference to Table 4 as a
scrivener’s error, and read it to cross-reference Table 16 of the Access
Amendments.

leads.caseName: Security First Insurance Company D/B/A Security First Florida v. Mark Annon and Amy Annon
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
FIFTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL
 STATE OF FLORIDA
 _____________________________

 Case No. 5D2025-1458
 LT Case No. 2021-CA-000558
 _____________________________

SECURITY FIRST INSURANCE
COMPANY D/B/A SECURITY FIRST
FLORIDA,

 Appellant,

 v.

MARK ANNON AND AMY ANNON,

 Appellees.
 _____________________________

On appeal from the Circuit Court for Flagler County.
Andrea K. Totten, Judge.

Michael Fox Orr and Loreyn P. Raab, of Orr Cook, Jacksonville,
for Appellant.

Michael Ciocchetti, of Michael Ciocchetti, PLLC, Daytona Beach,
for Appellee.

 October 9, 2026

LAMBERT, J.

 Security First Insurance Company (“Security First”), which
was the defendant below in a first-party property dispute that was
resolved without a trial, timely appeals the trial court’s
subsequent final judgment that awarded attorney’s fees against it
 under section 627.428, Florida Statutes (2021), 1 in favor of the
appellees/insureds, Mark Annon and Amy Annon. Consistent with
Florida Patient’s Compensation Fund v. Rowe, 472 So. 2d 1145
(Fla. 1985), the trial court first computed and then awarded to
Appellees in its final judgment the lodestar amount of $125,080.00
for attorney’s fees, which Security First has not challenged in this
appeal. The court then applied a 2.0 contingency fee multiplier to
this lodestar figure, resulting in an attorney’s fees award to
Appellees totaling $250,160.00, with which Security First does
take issue.

 Security First primarily argues that the 2.0 multiplier award
should be reversed because it is not supported by competent
substantial evidence. Concluding that Security First is correct, we
reverse the final judgment and remand with instructions to the
trial court to enter an amended final judgment that awards the
lodestar attorney’s fees sum of $125,080.00 to Appellees, without
a multiplier.
 I

 In Standard Guaranty Insurance v. Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d
828 (Fla. 1990), the Florida Supreme Court set forth the following
three factors to be utilized by courts when determining whether a
multiplier is necessary in the instant type of case:

 (1) whether the relevant market requires a
 contingency fee multiplier to obtain competent
 counsel; (2) whether the attorney was able to mitigate
 the risk of nonpayment in any way; and (3) whether
 any of the factors set forth in Rowe are applicable,
 especially, the amount involved, the results obtained,
 and the type of fee arrangement between the attorney
 and [the] client.

Id. at 834.

 1 Section 627.428, Florida Statutes, which permitted an award

of attorney’s fees in this type of case, was repealed in 2023. The
claim in this case pre-dates the repeal.

 2
  As the party seeking attorney’s fees, Appellees had the
burden to establish each of these factors to justify the contingency
fee multiplier. See Foot & Ankle Ctr. of Fla., LLC, v. Vargas, 412
So. 3d 825, 828 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024) (citing Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d
at 834). And “[w]hile the trial court’s determination to apply a
multiplier to the lodestar amount is reviewed for an abuse of
discretion, the trial court’s findings as to the multiplier must be
supported by competent, substantial evidence.” Universal Prop. &
Cas. Ins. v. Deshpande, 314 So. 3d 416, 420 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)
(citation omitted).

 II

 In arguing that the trial court’s application of the 2.0
contingency fee multiplier was not supported by competent
substantial evidence, Security First contends that Appellees failed
to meet their burden of presenting evidence sufficient to prove that
the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to obtain
competent counsel in this case. See SafePoint Ins. v. Castellanos,
394 So. 3d 731, 735 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (“If there is no evidence
that the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to
obtain competent counsel, then a multiplier should not be
awarded.” (citation omitted)).

 Security First also contends that the trial court’s finding on
the second prong or factor in Quanstrom, that Appellees’ counsel
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way, lacks
record evidentiary support.

 To establish the first factor under Quanstrom, Appellees
were required to demonstrate, without inference, that they would
have faced substantial difficulties in obtaining competent counsel
in the relevant market without the risk-enhancement multiplier.
See Little v. Bath & Kitchen Boutique, LLC, 435 So. 3d 1142, 1150
(Fla. 3d DCA 2026) (citing Foot & Ankle, 412 So. 3d at 829).

 Appellees did not testify at the attorney’s fees hearing; and
their expert witness, who admitted under oath that he did not
handle first-party property insurance cases such as the instant
claim nor did he speak with Appellees, testified that he made no
inquiry as to whether any other attorneys would have accepted

 3
 this type of case without the possibility of a contingency fee
multiplier. See Impex Caribe Corp. v. Carl Levin, P.A., 338 So. 3d
13, 15 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (recognizing that the party seeking
application of the multiplier “must establish ‘that a party would
have difficulty securing counsel without the opportunity for a
multiplier’” (quoting Citizens Prop. Ins. v. Laguerre, 259 So. 3d
169, 177 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018))); see also Bankers Life & Cas. v.
Borew, 430 So. 3d 124, 128 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (“So, to award the
multiplier, the record evidence must show that without risk-
enhancement[,] plaintiff would have faced substantial difficulties
in finding counsel in the . . . relevant market.” (alteration in
original) (citation omitted)).

 Instructive on this issue is this court’s decision in PHH
Mortgage Corp. v. Schreiber, 397 So. 3d 1159 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024),
where the appellant challenged an attorney’s fees award with a
contingency fee multiplier in a foreclosure case. Id. at 1159. The
appellees’ expert there testified that for “almost all [foreclosure]
clients, because they couldn’t pay their mortgage, they can’t pay
their attorney or . . . they pay very little as compared to the amount
of work involved.” Id. at 1160 (alteration in original). The expert
further opined that, because of the client’s inability to pay, most
foreclosures involved some type of contingency fee. Id.

 Concluding that this testimony said nothing about whether a
foreclosure client could have obtained competent counsel without
a multiplier, we reversed and remanded for entry of an amended
judgment without the contingency multiplier. Id.

 Appellees’ expert’s testimony here was similarly lacking as to
whether Appellees could have obtained competent counsel in the
relevant market absent the possibility of a multiplier. We
therefore hold, without further elaboration, that Appellees failed
to meet their evidentiary burden under the first Quanstrom factor
to support the imposition of the contingency risk multiplier.

 III

 We further find that Appellees did not present competent
substantial evidence of the second Quanstrom factor that counsel
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way.

 4
 “Generally, the controlling consideration in determining whether
an attorney can mitigate the risk of nonpayment . . . is whether the
plaintiffs can afford a retainer or hourly fees.” Certain
Underwriters at Lloyd’s London v. Candelaria, 339 So. 3d 463, 470
(Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (quoting Wesson v. Fla. Peninsula Ins., 296 So.
3d 572, 573 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020)). Simply stated, there was no
specific, non-inferential evidence before the trial court that
Appellees could not have afforded or lacked the financial means to
either pay a retainer fee or counsel’s hourly rate.

 Accordingly, we conclude that the trial court erred in applying
the 2.0 contingency risk multiplier to the lodestar attorney’s fees
amount. We therefore reverse that portion of the final judgment
and remand with directions to the trial court to enter an amended
final judgment that awards to Appellees the $125,080.00 lodestar
attorney’s fees figure previously determined, with no multiplier. 2

 REVERSED and REMANDED with directions.

EDWARDS and BOATWRIGHT, JJ., concur.

 2 On a final note, effective March 24, 2023, the Florida
Legislature amended section 57.104, Florida Statutes, to provide
that “[i]n any action in which attorney fees are determined or
awarded by the court, there is a strong presumption that a lodestar
fee is sufficient and reasonable,” and that “[t]his presumption may
be overcome only in a rare and exceptional circumstance with
evidence that competent counsel could not otherwise be retained.”
§ 57.104(2), Fla. Stat. Security First’s second argument for
reversal here briefly argued that this statute should be applied
retroactively and that this was not the rare and exceptional case
to overcome the strong presumption that the lodestar fee awarded
was sufficient and reasonable.

 While the record in this appeal supports Security First’s
argument that this case was not rare and exceptional, based upon
our disposition of Security First’s first issue on appeal, we find it
unnecessary to address the retroactive applicability of section
57.104(2).
